utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Domazet: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Loncarevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall continue our conversation from yesterday and as far as I can recall, we stopped at the point when your patient Mitar Vasiljevic was due to be taken to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you personally remember who drove Mr. Vasiljevic to Uzice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when the vehicle left in the direction of Uzice or rather did you see that moment and do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, was Zivorad Savic one of the drivers at the health centre at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, Zivorad Savic was one of the drivers at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could he have been the driver who took Mitar Vasiljevic to Uzice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you whether you would see Mitar Vasiljevic in town, you said that you very rarely went to the centre of town because of your busy schedule and because you were living in a position which doesn't take you through the centre of town, but could you tell me whether this reason was the only one why you didn't go into the centre of town or was there any other reason why you avoided downtown Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I intentionally avoided the centre because it was only to be assumed that in wartime, and the situation such as it was at the time, I might encounter unpleasantness and be confronted with a situation I would rather avoid, and that is why I avoided going to the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The unpleasantness that you mention, could you tell us who they might originate from and who they did originate from, in fact, at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: They came from people, most of whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Loncarevic, that these were people who had come from out of Visegrad, who were not from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely what I had in mind. In fact, I did have some problems on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the problems you had for us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion, I was stopped by some men, there were a number of them, I don't remember exactly how many. I didn't know a single one of them. They were armed. They wore beards. They stopped me on my way to my house, the house I was born in, and they wanted to take all the fuel I had in the tank of my car after asking having asked me to show them my ID. The story ended by my fuel remaining intact after a great deal of discussion, but it was unpleasant. Also on another occasion at the new bridge, I was again stopped by a group of men. They could be described similarly as the previous group. They told me to follow them, and they took me to the Crnca neighbourhood where there were a few more of them and after examining my ID papers, they again wanted to take fuel from the car, but fortunately there was very little left in the car and after keeping me there for a while, they let me go back to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, you told us that those persons demanded to see your ID and on both cases, wanted to take your fuel. So I assume you showed them your ID?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well one wasn't allowed -- couldn't move around anywhere without an ID.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you at the start, though it's probably clear to everyone, but please tell us what ethnic group you belong to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: By ethnicity I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that obvious on the basis of your first and last name, the name of your father, and the other information contained in your ID?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, while working at the health centre, did you have a similar encounter to the one you just described in town?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. Where are we headed on this, Mr. Domazet? We've got no identification of the people who did this to him and if you are asking him to relate any more incidents of this, I don't see where we're going and, indeed, you will recall your undertaking not to go into detail if this is alleged to be an attack upon the Serbian civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I do not intend to prove any attack on the Serb population, but just to ask the witness a few questions. This was going to be the last one, relevant to the conduct and behaviour of paramilitaries in Visegrad at the time, and I think it is relevant for the case who these people were, whether they were from Visegrad or not, and whether, in addition to Muslims, they harassed other inhabitants of Visegrad and I think it is significant. I only have one further question regarding an incident in the medical centre itself with paramilitaries who were in Visegrad at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, there is no suggestion that these people were paramilitaries. If you want to prove that, I would agree with you, it is relevant and the fact that they harassed the Serbian population as well, but you haven't got any evidence of that. We can't guess at this sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from what the witness has said that these were armed men, the way they behaved, I think that follows that they were, but I shall rephrase the question accordingly, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. They were armed and they wore beards. Well, if you want us to take this into account, I think you might have to demonstrate just a little bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if this is the last one, I suppose we are going to have this by some process of attrition. I do want to get on with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Loncarevic, the people you encountered in town, were they wearing any uniforms of any kind?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what you saw the reservists wearing, would you say that these belonged to the regular military units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: They did not look like regular military men, nor did they behave like regular soldiers. Most of them wore camouflage uniforms, some wore black uniforms, some had -- most of them had beards, some had bandannas, cockades, magazines across their chests, and they were heavily armed and they didn't resemble in any way a regular army by appearance or by their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one further point since you had direct contact with them and you spoke with them, do you remember whether you could tell by the way they spoke their dialect, where these people came from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: May I answer this question for security reasons, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's up to you. If you feel that could put your safety at risk, I will ask for us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I'll answer the question nevertheless. These were not men from Bosnia. I, of course, have no proof, but I don't think they were from Bosnia. I assume that they were men from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncarevic. One further question: Did you personally experience an encounter in the health centre itself with people similar to those you had just described?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please describe the incident for us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: There were several. I remember a number of occasions when they would, among other places, come to the health centre and they did not show a minimum of respect towards the staff. They were rude, prone to violence and aggression. They usurped our space. They disturbed us. They would sit on our chairs and beds. We had nowhere to sit or lie down. Sometimes we had to spend the whole night on our feet because they were resting and we didn't dare utter a single word of protest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncarevic. Let me move on now. After the day you described, the day when Mitar Vasiljevic left, you continued working in the Uzice -- sorry, in the Visegrad health centre. Could you tell me, please, until when you continued working and were there any interruptions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: After Mitar Vasiljevic was taken to hospital, I did have an interruption because of an injury. Actually, it was self-inflicted by myself with my own pistol. It happened on the 24th of June, 1992 when I, too, went to the surgery ward of the Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you, yourself, Dr. Loncarevic, stay at the Uzice hospital undergoing treatment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: From the 31st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself, until the 31st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the Uzice hospital, did you see Mitar Vasiljevic in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I knew that Mitar Vasiljevic was in another wing of the hospital right opposite mine, and as soon as I became mobile, I went to the room where Mitar Vasiljevic was lying and paid him a brief visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said as soon as you were mobile, can you remember how many days that was after your arrival at the Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: About two to three days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ward that you said was in the wing opposite yours, what ward was it at which Mitar Vasiljevic was being treated at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: It was the orthopaedics ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him or come across him any other time while you were in hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I did come across him a few days later, I don't remember exactly how many days later, but anyway, during my stay at the hospital we met in the hospital hall close to the telephone box, and we exchanged a few words, but we parted quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you remember the conversation you had or anything special about that conversation with Mitar at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: It stuck in my mind because Mitar was not speaking very logically when we met. He didn't quite understand why I was there, so it was rather difficult to communicate with him and that is why I didn't insist and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. spend much time with him. He had a plaster cast on his leg with drawings and names and letters scribbled all over it so I didn't want to stay any longer with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you didn't want to stay with him, does that mean that you avoided continuing the conversation, you wanted to end it quickly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the correct understanding of what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that second occasion, you told us that he had a plaster cast and some drawings on it and some stickers on it, how was he moving around when you saw him on that second occasion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: He was in a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time you saw him in his room, Mr. Loncarevic, do you remember what that encounter was like or rather what position he was in? Could you tell us a few more words about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I think he was lying in bed immobile with a traction, with weights on his leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other patients in that room, were there several beds in that room; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a room with several beds in it. I don't remember who the people in the room with Mitar were, but I think that a patient, a Muslim patient whose surname was Lepenica was in the same room as Mitar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Loncarevic, that at the time you came across some other people from Visegrad who were also in hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met some other people who were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of some of them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I would see Slavko Trifkovic, Miroslav Mirkovic, Dragan Filipovic, a policeman known as Rakila [as interpreted], I don't know his proper name even now. They still call him Rakila and some others whose names don't occur to me just now. Excuse me, I said Rakela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that you stayed in the hospital until the 31st of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you told us that you saw Mitar only twice, do you nevertheless know until when Mitar stayed in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid I can't say exactly, but I think he left before me, but I am not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, do you perhaps have on you any evidence to prove that you were in the hospital during the period you have indicated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I have the discharge paper from the hospital on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do have it on you, would you be kind enough to read the name of your case history from that discharge document, if you could, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The number on the discharge document is 1060710607.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncarevic. When you were describing the period and the circumstances surrounding Mitar Vasiljevic's injury to the best of your recollection, you told us as much as you remembered. In those days, you probably had a lot to do, you were very busy, you had a large number of patients; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were many patients and many activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us why it is that you remember what you do regarding the admission of Mitar Vasiljevic at the health centre in Visegrad or, rather, in view of the time that has gone by, how it is that you remember those details?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I probably would not remember Mitar as I don't many other patients that I treated, but Mitar's case was indeed unusual. Even in the course of my schooling or career, after that, I never had a case of somebody having an injury inflicted as a result of horse riding. There are not that many horses and horse riders in our area and as this was my only case of such an injury with a horse, that is probably the reason why I still remember some details regarding the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you make a statement to Mr. Tanaskovic, an attorney from Visegrad, in connection with this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did make a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that in that statement, you said, when describing this event, that you wouldn't know the date but that you established it on the basis of the official record and it was then that you said that it was on the 14th of June, 1992. Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is the value of an answer to a leading question like that, Mr. Domazet? It would be more impressive if he produced the official records or a copy of them so we could have a look at the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is just what I intend to do, Your Honour. That is exactly my intention and I wish to tender these records into evidence, the records mentioned by Mr. Loncarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I get the impression that we are going slower with this witness than we've gone with any witness in this case. There must be some limit to it. Will you please go to the relevant thing, ask him to have a look at it, say that they are the official records and they can be tendered or a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please, let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, please tell me how records were kept on patients who came to the health centre asking for help?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the basic details were entered on the left page of the protocol, that was where the nurse entered information and the diagnosis, therapy, and other notes were entered on the right-hand page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did doctors write anything in this book?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Doctors mostly wrote the diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, I will now show you a book and ask you to look at it and tell us whether you recognise it and if you do, tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I request that this book be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is the records book of the Visegrad health centre of patients for the time period that can be seen on the cover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please read us what it says on the cover of the book. First of all, the title, and then whether there are any handwritten notes on the book?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The title is, "Protocol of Outpatients," and by hand it says, "First-aid ward from 3821 on from the 20th of April 1992 until the 4th of July 1992."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the book into which all the patients treated in the first-aid ward in the period mentioned by you from the 20th of April to the 4th of July, 1992 were entered?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is that book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, this book begins with 3821?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please find number 5353 in this book.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I have found number 5353.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please read to the Court what you can conclude from this entry, entry 5353. First of all, tell us the date and whether this can be seen from the records.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: In the book, we can see that the date is the 14th of June. The patient is Mitar Vasiljevic. He was born in 1954. He comes from Visegrad, a member of the Territorial Defence, and that's what it says, diagnosis, fracture. The therapy administered, eraglandrodom [phoen] 50 milligrams, glucose and then he was referred to the orthopaedic ward in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Under entry number 5354 and 5355, are these also patients who were received and examined on the same day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The basis of these records, it would appear to be so. I can't recall that, but that's what it says in the records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at number 5597 in the book.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: 5597, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date and what the injury is about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The date is the 24th of June, 1992. Goran Loncarevic from Visegrad. Diagnosis, wounds: Vulnus sclopetarium thoracis lat. dex. Therapy: Infusion, referred to the surgical ward in Uzice and he was given an injection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it you, Mr. Loncarevic, who entered this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the case you described, the reason you were referred to the Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Loncarevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What do you want done with the book, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There are copies provided so we don't want the original but how are you going to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender the original as evidence because some other witnesses perhaps might be able to look at the original. I therefore propose that both the copies and the original be entered into evidence as VGD26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I assume the book is no longer in use.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly it was brought by the director of the health centre who will testify here, Dr. Vasiljevic, and we shall be able to ask him. I hope there will be no obstacle to this book remaining here for a certain time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this case, the Defence triggered reciprocal discovery and I would like to let you know we never saw this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I am not aware of those sorts of things. Are you objecting to the tender?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: We would like to have an opportunity to examine just over the break or the original of the document because it's the first time that we get hold of it. Despite requesting it already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you not seen a copy of it before?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No, neither. That's exactly what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why is that, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It seems almost like a conspiracy to slow the process of this case down. I'm getting very, very, annoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why wasn't it shown to the Prosecution earlier than this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This book was brought to The Hague by Dr. Radomir Vasiljevic, a witness, who is the present director of the health centre. He brought the original here, and he, himself, signed the receipt which I entered into the materials and which has been described, describing all the situations in 1992 when Mitar Vasiljevic was entered into the records and the entry under 5353 of the 14th of June is part of this material so it has been disclosed. The only thing we did not have was the original because I, myself, did not dare ask for the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, are you suggesting that a copy of this was produced to the Prosecution before today?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a copy of the whole book, but a report on what dates and under what numbers Mitar Vasiljevic was entered into the records in 1992, and this was disclosed with the other potential evidence of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When did Dr. Vasiljevic arrive in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, but I saw him two days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, why hasn't a copy of this been given to the Prosecution? Can't you see that this is the only way trials here can work? You are required to produce copies of exhibits in advance. Anyway, we'll look at it again after lunch but it's going to have to go in then and it's only a matter of weight that you could attack it on. It's been properly identified. There's no reason why it should not go into evidence. Yes, now are there any more questions you want to ask of the doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, please. Cross-examined by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Loncarevic. I'm counsel appearing for the Prosecution and I'd like to ask you several questions this morning. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yesterday, you told us and correct me if I am wrong that you were actually mobilised into the army and assigned to the Visegrad health centre; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I was actually mobilised or simply assigned to work duty, but in any case, I was assigned to the health centre and I had orders to stay there until further notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told us yesterday that you were one of three so-called able-bodied men who had to work basically around the clock in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be correct in assuming that you, at the minimum, saw about ten people a day in the health centre during those times?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: More than ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, definitely it would make up to 70 to 100 a week, would you agree with that estimate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I would agree with the estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also told us yesterday that the first or the vague memory you had of when Mr. Vasiljevic was brought in is when he was carried on a stretcher to the x-ray room; is this right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that was inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not inside the hospital because the x-ray room is reached by an outside staircase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you describe you accompanied the injured Mitar Vasiljevic to the x-ray room on this outside staircase?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that, and that is the clearest image that sticks in my memory because it was on the way to the x-ray room that I found out some of the details about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in order -- you told us today, in order to basically with so many people attend, if you had to attend to, the only way to really say when Mr. Vasiljevic came in at what time is to rely on medical records; would you agree with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I really could not be certain about the time, but only about the date. I am sure about the date, but as for the rest, I would have to rely on the records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's probably now a confusion in the record. You said you can't be sure about the date and you would have to rely on the record or are you sure about the date without the record? I think there was a bit of confusion in the record now.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: It's possible there has been some confusion. No, I never said I was certain about the date. I can only tell you the date on the basis of the records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the records, wouldn't it be sort of general practice if somebody's brought to a hospital to also indicate a time of admission to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the usual practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me try to understand you. If an accident occurred and somebody would come to an emergency room and would be administered first aid and some medicine, wouldn't it be very vital for the subsequent treatment to indicate the time the person was brought into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, possibly that would have been a better way of proceeding, but even today we do not enter the time someone is admitted and especially then, I'm trying to explain that the conditions were very bad and we had practically no instructions for our work. Most of us did what we could on our own initiative and even the information we have is a lot, considering the terrible conditions we had to work in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you if somebody was dead and was brought in dead, wouldn't you then enter the time of death into the record as the time of the admission?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in that case it would be written down, it was done then and it's still done today and that is the general practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can I get you to agree with me that basically the record was at least incomplete as regards to the time somebody is admitted, admissioned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on this. I think it falls within the sphere of legal interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, -- well then, let's stick to the medical interpretation. You told us that yesterday that an x-ray had to be taken from two different angles because, as you said, it's a hard and fast rule in order to get the information regarding the type and time of injury. Now --

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you then not, in any kind of medical record, be it the referral document or the admissions document, indicate at least a time and type of the injury?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that it would have been a good thing had it been done, and that in general, it would be the proper thing to do, but at that time, referral notes were not written out and the time was not entered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I guess I got you again wrong there. You said yesterday that a referral was obligatory because otherwise a patient wouldn't have been able to be accepted in the hospital so a referral was written out, only the time wasn't written out?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: When I spoke of the referral note, I was talking about the hospital in Uzice. He would not have been admitted to the hospital in Uzice without a referral. I understood you to ask me about the referral for the x-ray in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I was talking about the referral note. What I'm actually interested in is whether you or anybody else you instructed ever put down either on a referral note to the Uzice hospital or in any other medical record of the health care centre in Visegrad a time and the type of the injury?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I said yesterday I didn't know who wrote out the referral note, it may have been me, but I can't be sure because I don't know now. Whoever wrote out the referral note had to put in the name of the institution to which the patient was being referred and the diagnosis, that is the type of injury. This referral note was also the document on the basis of which the patient was provided with transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic fractured his leg. Isn't it quite important for a fracture, medically speaking, when the fracture actually occurred? Because isn't it important for the treatment after, whether the fracture is an old fracture, let's say, of ten hours or whether the fracture was a very recent fracture; wouldn't that make a difference in the application of the treatment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I understood your question fully, but if I am wrong, please correct me. As far as I am concerned, there was no dilemma in my mind as to when the fracture had occurred, because I was told that he had just recently fallen off a horse. As for the orthopaedic surgeon, for them it would be important to know the time and an orthopaedic surgeon could give you more information about that because I am not a specialist for orthopaedic matters but that simply was not noted down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there ever a copy kept from the referral document, because it is basically a very detailed document, or is the only information you have about the patient in the protocol of the health care centre?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: There are never any copies of the referral note. The referral note is sent to the medical institution where the patient is being treated and then they forward that referral to the health insurance fund for compensation of costs so that the health centre does not have a copy and it would be right to say that this protocol is the only document where there are written -- where there is written information about this patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And wouldn't on this referral document also the cause of the injury be noted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: It is not customary to indicate the cause of the injury in the referral note.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So basically the health insurance then doesn't have any idea whether something, an accident occurred as part of the work obligation or as part of private pleasure, let's say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but for our system of health insurance, that was not important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even if you would have broken your leg playing football or any other activity which was not part of anything, the health insurance would have covered it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I have to say with some reserve, because I am not an expert, but in those days, treatment was free of charge in our country regardless of the cause of the disease or the injury, and the medical insurance fund did not verify these things. It was only important for the company in question because compensation for absence from work depended on the way in which the patient had fallen ill or had got hurt, and it was important later for disability benefits or any other benefits that may have been claimed. But for the treatment itself, it was not important. Please forgive me if what I am saying is not 100 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I understand you correctly, for the claim of an insurance, it wouldn't have mattered actually if on insurance document or a document that was provided to the insurance, it would have noted whether Mr. Vasiljevic fell off a horse or whether he injured himself on the battle field; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: It would not be important. The insurance would even cover injuries provoked under the influence of alcohol and any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Dr. Loncarevic, when the x-ray was taken before you probably instructed or filled yourself out the referral letter, you probably took a look at the x-ray, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I would have had to have a look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: But I really do not remember whether I actually did, but I probably did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you described as quite detailed what is all on the x-ray. I would like to show you a document and it is the original -- said to be the original x-ray and I would like only to see whether you could identify that this might have been the original x-ray you took of Mitar Vasiljevic's leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: The number is pre-numbered 151.1.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, may I make a correction? I didn't describe the film in detail, I just said what is indicated on the film, the name, surname, the date, and what side the film has been taken from and that this was indicated with a marker. I didn't give any other details about the x-ray, but I will have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncarevic -- sorry, I just had one specific question whether you identify that this is the type of x-rays you would have done in the health care centre in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Actually you asked him specifically was that the x-ray taken at the -- at his hospital. That's a slightly different question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I agree. I wanted first to see whether he can at all identify it as an x-ray which is sort of the form of the x-ray they took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, no. Do you want him to identify that as the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one taken at his hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes. And then whether he can recollect whether this could be the x-ray, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the question you're being asked, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: This resembles the format of x-rays. I didn't say that I could recognise an x-ray, but I do not think that this could be the one, the one you have given me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't recognise the handwriting or anything else on it which would sort of indicate or the way it is written which would indicate that was the usual procedure applied to in 1992 in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I do not recognise the handwriting and other details I probably would not recognise anyway, but all in all, it is not probable that that is it. The handwriting is not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else that seems not right on it or ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: There is a plaster longette on this leg, not plaster, I'm sorry, a metal longette. I am not sure that Mitar had such a longette at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncarevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you may know Ms. Bauer, but I don't, what is a metal longette, doctor, is that the frame that you can see in the x-ray?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, it's a metal netting adjusted in such a way as to be formed according to the shape of the extremity. It is adjustable to the shape of the extremity

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And it's to keep the bones in place, I assume, it is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is its purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, one further question, doctor, there is an indication handwritten which is called "god" or what does it mean, after the 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: This is "god" which is short for godina which means year in Latinic script, g-o-d short for year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncarevic. I think it can be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Was that not tendered in evidence when Dr. De Grave gave his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: As far as I understood, it was a copy of the original but it wasn't the original, original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know the Prosecution has certain views about who owns the exhibits in these cases, but it should not be left with a copy if this is going to be important, we should have the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, I'm prepared to tender it. I thought only because the witness doesn't identify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, we'll have to -- but you'll have to deal with it at some stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was one other question I was made aware of. As soon as x-rays are taken, is it a practice to label them right there once they are developed or are they going to be labelled later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The x-rays are first dried and then immediately the information is written on to the film, as soon as the film has dried.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'd like that the doctor looks at the Exhibit D22.1. I have copies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncarevic, do you recognise any of those names listed on this list? And please, don't refer to the names if you do recognise one, but to their numbers which are associated on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise some people on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So without telling me the names, could you just tell me which VGD numbers you do recognise?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I know the person VGD7, also VGD10, also VGD12, VGD16, VGD18, VGD19, VGD20, and I think I also know the person under VGD14 if it is the same person that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, any of these people, have you had to treat them for any injuries in the health care centre during this time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that VGD7 came because she [as interpreted] had kidney trouble. I think she had a stone in her kidney, and as far as I can remember, I think she also went to the military medical academy in Belgrade for treatment for this problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncarevic one clarifying question, is this a female, according to you, or a male?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: VGD7 is a male.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's because the record was reflecting "she" so I just wanted to clarify that. Now, we have heard evidence that some of these people were part of a paramilitary group and could you -- would you have seen them in the company of paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, the paramilitary groups I came across most often in the medical centre and not anywhere else, and these persons that I mentioned came alone to the institution I work in. So I can't claim with any certainty that they belonged to a paramilitary group, but it's quite -- I don't exclude the possibility that they -- some of them were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, because today, one thing caught my attention, you said, "I didn't know most of them," which would indicate to me that you might have known some of the paramilitaries. Would that be a correct assumption?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I was speaking about other people, people that do not figure on this list. They were people that I saw for the first time in my life, and whom I absolutely did not know and they moved around in groups. As for these people on this list, some of them I do know and they came individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you couldn't exclude that they were associated with paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I do not exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, did you have -- I'm sure you did have TV stations in Visegrad, what kind of TV stations could you receive during wartime?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I had very little time to watch TV. For long stretches, we didn't have any electricity. As far as I can recall, in those days, we could watch, that is, until the war really escalated, we could watch one Sarajevo station and one Belgrade station. Later on, I really don't know, I think we also had a local TV programme. I don't know when it started and for how long it lasted, but I do think that it existed but as I was saying, I personally had really hardly any time to watch television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after the war broke out, you couldn't receive Sarajevo TV anymore; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure of that. That may be right but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you wouldn't have seen any report about a fire on the 14th of June in Visegrad on any of the TV stations, would you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything like that, and it may sound hard to believe, to this day, I am not familiar with any details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to look as a conclusion at two entries in the book and I think I have the two entries marked up here. The first entry is 4951 and the other one is 5270. It's regarding a person called Dragan Tomic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you say 4971.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I find the name Dragan Tomic born in 1957 in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please maybe tell us what is the diagnosis or what it is says in the column 13?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Column number 13, there's no diagnosis. It says doctor's examination and an electrocardiogram which means that the doctor examined him and had his electrocardiogram taken. There's no other information as far as I can see except in column 7, "MKP," and I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next number is 5270 also regarding Mr. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dragan Tomic, born 1959 in Visegrad, and there is more information here, registration number, the code for the area of activity, and his ID number and it says, "Attached to the Territorial Defence with enterprise Varda," the diagnosis is 462 and 466 and I think that in those days, these are old codes from the international classification of disease which I have almost forgotten but I think that 462 meant tonsillitis. The other code I don't recognise. He was given antibiotic injections garamycin, 20 milligrams; ascorbic acid, that is vitamin C; ibedoxin, 50 milligrams; and some other medicines. It's not indicated whether it was intravenously or in the muscle. He was given this injection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Loncarevic, in connection with this last question put to you by the Prosecution, will you look at these two entries once again. The first is 4951?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You will have noticed of course they had different years of birth, they obviously are unlikely to be the same people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this, I very nearly asked the Prosecution, what is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: As far as I can get, Your Honour, we just tried to figure out because Dragan Tomic features in the evidence and he is supposed to be dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know, but it is not the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, there were two persons so I had to ask either of them to figure out whether there is a death notice in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Obviously not. Now that's the relevance of the Prosecution. Do you think that you really do need to ask any questions about it in re-examination? Unless he died of tonsillitis, I don't see what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is two questions, Your Honour. Just two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 4951 nothing more is indicated except the year of birth and Mr. Loncarevic, you said you don't understand what "MKB" is, but if we were to read it as MUP, then would you recognise what it stands for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could be read as "MUP" if the letter in the middle is a U which in case it is the Ministry of Internal Affairs, in short, the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the second entry, 5270 where there is more information, you said that that person was insured through the Varda company?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say that he was insured through the Varda company but that he belonged to Varda which usually meant that he worked there because that was the custom if somebody was employed somewhere, he would be assigned to that company. 012310, that is the field of activity, the code for the field of activity and one can check whether Varda, that company, had this code because Varda was the company the patient was employed in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of what you have just said and the years of birth in the first and the second case, can you infer from that whether it is the same person or could it be two different persons with the same first and last names?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: As we see that the years of birth differ, to say the least, it is quite clear that these are two different persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to Ms. Bauer's question about the metal longette, my question is: Did you or someone else carry out the immobilisation of Mitar Vasiljevic on that day before he was sent on to Uzice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Somebody had to do the immobilisation. I truly do not remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does immobilisation include the placement of this metal longette?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it means administering the metal longette or anything else that can immobilise the joints close to the fracture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us what your specialty is in medicine, did you ever specialise orthopaedics?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I never specialised in orthopaedics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of your other colleagues who were working with you at the time orthopaedic surgeons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no orthopaedic surgeon working with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question in this connection, would it be right to say that immobilisation had to be done but that you don't remember who did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it, whether it was you or one of your colleagues, did I understand your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, this was the first-aid department, I think you described it as, that this book was kept by. If somebody is being dealt with as an outpatient who comes from day to day, is there -- would you expect there to be an entry for that person each day that they attended?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I would expect there to be an entry for every day, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want to ask any questions about that, Ms. Bauer?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just one question. Further Re-examination by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those days in the health centre, was there any other book of records for the examination of patients in addition to this one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: I cannot assert with certainty whether there was or not. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Doctor, I have one question. Please look up the medical book which was extended by Defence counsel number 5332.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: 5332, the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: The surname is not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: It's illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: The second column and the third column it is written 14.6. It means that June 14th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: If the date hasn't been written before, and if this is the first time it was written, it means that this happened on the 14th of June, 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: The handwriting of the second and third column, that means 14.6 is very different for me, seems like very different for me from the other handwriting, the first column, the fourth column, et cetera et cetera, so I have one question: When and by whom those figures, the second and third column, were written?

utterances.speaker: GORAN LONCAREVIC
utterances.text: Who wrote them down and when, I don't know, but it is the nurses who are responsible for writing down the date and I said at the beginning of my testimony that the whole left page of the protocol would be filled in by nurses so it must have been one of the nurses. Why it's somewhat different, I am really unable to say. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does either counsel want to ask any questions arising out of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor, for coming along to give your evidence and for the evidence you've given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too for inviting me to come and for giving me a chance to contribute to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will resume again at 11.35 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might before we begin this witness, on the break I spoke with Mr. Domazet and by agreement, we would like to tender the original x-ray now as Prosecution Exhibit 151.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is 151 the photostat of it, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. That will be Exhibit P151.1. Now, sir, would you stand up please and make the solemn declaration in the document in which the court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Tanaskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To begin with, would you please tell us your full name, your date of birth and your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Miloje Novakovic. I was born on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the year?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In the municipality of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll need the year, the interpreter didn't hear it, Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, would you tell us where you reside now?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I now live in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been living in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have been living in Visegrad since 1948.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what school you completed and what your occupation is?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed a two-year post secondary school for economics and I work in the health centre in Visegrad as head of finance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been employed in the Visegrad health centre?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have been working in the Visegrad health centre since the 12th of August, 1962.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work in the health centre during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, during the war, and I still work there today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, were you assigned to the health centre as part of a work duty or other kind of duty?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned there on the basis of my work obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in the beginning that you live in Visegrad. For the purposes of my next question, would you please tell us the street where you live?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Kralja Petra I Street, number 4 in Visegrad which is, in fact, the main street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of this street before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was called Marsala Tita Street, the house number was the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what route you took to get from your house to the health centre where you worked?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The street I live in is on the right bank of the River Drina, the health centre is on the left bank. Therefore, I had to cross the bridge, go down the street and cross the bridge in order to get to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the street" you are referring to Marsala Tita Street later renamed King Peter Street?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mitar because he comes from Visegrad and he used to work in a catering establishment in the Panos company in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of catering establishment, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was a waiter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know him both as a fellow citizen and as a waiter?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you used to go from your flat or house in the direction of the health centre, that is, on your way to work, did you see Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I usually drove to work and it was usually at 8.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you would see Mr. Vasiljevic, can you tell us what he was doing at those times when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were lots of broken shop windows, a lot of garbage, a lot of rubbish all over the town and he said that he was organising the cleaning of the town. He would tour the streets with the people who worked in the shops and other people who are probably unemployed or pensioners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that until then, no one had cleaned the town?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. No one had cleaned it because the utility company whose job it was to take care of garbage disposal was not operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you remember the persons working with Mr. Vasiljevic, were they Serbs, Muslims, or members of some third ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: There were both Serbs and Muslims. There were people who happened to be there or people who were recruited to do the job as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, as a citizen of Visegrad, were you satisfied with the appearance of the streets they cleaned or rather that they had cleaned?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I was. As I said, there was shattered glass everywhere, there was rubbish scattered about and they took care of the cleanliness of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this just your opinion or do you know that others shared this opinion?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all of us who lived there shared this opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would see Mr. Vasiljevic, can you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I always saw him wearing civilian clothes. It was a suit of dark coloured suit of clothes and on one occasion, I remember seeing him wearing some sort of T-shirt or track suit and sneakers, as far as I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that one occasion when you saw him in a track suit and tennis shoes, you said that he was wearing something dark on the top of his body?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I said that the clothes he wore were dark usually, but on that occasion, he was wearing a T-shirt with short sleeves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you would see him, whether he wore any sort of symbol or something that was noticeable, that distinguished him?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he wore an armband. It was red, but I don't remember whether it had any symbols on it, I just remember that it was red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand this armband that you saw on Vasiljevic's arm to mean?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. To me, it meant that he had been assigned to the job he was doing probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us until when you saw Vasiljevic doing this?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was before he broke his leg and before he was transported away, maybe some ten days or so. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I understand your answer to mean that you used to see him doing this for about ten days before he broke his leg? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: According to me, it was in early June. I don't remember the exact day, but it was some ten days. I can't tell you any dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have now said until he broke his leg, what can you tell us about this and how do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know because I was at home. I had just come back from work, and I was resting. It was in the afternoon. I had told the drivers in the health centre, because I had some problems with my eyes and my blood pressure, I had asked them that if they were going to Uzice, I would go with them if it was possible for a check-up, and I wasn't too sure when I would be able to go there because of the passage to Uzice. I got a phone call from the driver Savic, nicknamed Zika and he said to me, "Mitar has fallen off his horse and broken his leg." And he asked me if I would go with him, he had a free seat in his ambulance and he wanted me to accompany him because he didn't like driving there on his own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was then that you learned that Mr. Vasiljevic had broken his leg?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that Mr. Savic told you something else about your departure?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: He said he would let me know when he set out in view of the fact that first aid had to be administered to Mitar and they would have to wait for a vehicle to be available and he said he would ring me up or rather that he would ring my doorbell when he came to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Savic did not tell you at what time he would come by?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he just said it wouldn't be right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how much time elapsed, at least approximately, before Mr. Savic came by with his vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe 40 minutes or an hour, something between 40 minutes and an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you lay eyes on Mr. Vasiljevic for the first time on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle stopped in front of the house where I live, I came down the stairs. I got into the vehicle and I saw Mr. Vasiljevic lying on a stretcher in the back of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then set out towards the hospital in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we set out towards the hospital in Uzice. I remember well that it was raining and that it was a winding road, there were rocks on the road, so we -- land slides, so we couldn't really drive fast. And when we arrived at Vardiste, Mitar asked us to stop at the Sikiric cafe because his uncle and aunt were there, because he was cold, and also for us to take some refreshments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, would you please wait for me to complete my question. When you set out from Visegrad, can you tell us what time it was, approximately, and if you can't tell us this, could you at least try to tell us approximately what time it was?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was still daylight but it was dark because of the rain and the clouds. It was misty. There was rain falling, drizzling, I don't know. It was sometime between 1630 [as interpreted] or 1900, 1830 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was still daylight?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see in the transcript that perhaps it's a mistake so I have to go back and ask you again, at what time you said it was that you set out because I may have misheard or there may be a mistake in the transcript. Could you please repeat what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you the exact time, but it could have been between 1830 and 19 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says in the transcript 1630 instead of 1830.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that the road was wet, that it was raining, that there were landslides. What about the safety situation, how safe was the Visegrad to Vardiste strip of road?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't safe because there were ambushes by the Muslims so it wasn't safe to travel along that road both because of the condition of the road, there was no maintenance at all, and because of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Novakovic, so we've got as far as Vardiste, and you've dropped in to see Sikiric, that is Mr. Vasiljevic's uncle. Did you go inside to see Mr. Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we went in to the coffee bar, he was inside, and we sat down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the word "establishment," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Coffee bar, restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the name of that establishment, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you told us, you told Mr. Sikiric what had happened, and did you have a drink or not?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I and Mr. Zivorad had a drink inside, and they took a drink for him into the car because he couldn't come out and he was complaining that he was cold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know what Mr. Vasiljevic drank, what it was that his uncle gave him, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was his uncle or his aunt, but I don't know what the drink was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say, how long did you stay there in that catering establishment?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Between 20 minutes and half an hour, not longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any problems crossing the borders or was it just a check-up?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we would always have to stop to show our documents, to tell them where we were going at both crossing, so this took some time, you see. I can't say how long, but we had to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, if you remember, tell us exactly if you know when that would be even better or approximately when you arrived at the Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: We were in Uzice about 2100 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you perhaps present together with Mr. Savic when he was handing over the patient, Mr. Vasiljevic, to the admissions department at the Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. A person comes out to take over the patient, and I immediately went to the eye department, to the eye ward, ophthalmology department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember how much later you left the hospital to return to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I spent about between 10 and 15 minutes at each ward so I stayed between 20 and 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Vasiljevic stayed behind at the hospital in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how much time Mr. Vasiljevic spent at the hospital in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much, but I would see him later on, I don't know when it was I saw him again. I saw him with crutches and I know he came to the health centre to change his bandages, but I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would see him when he came to the health centre for check-ups?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was on crutches at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you said that you knew Mr. Vasiljevic both as a waiter and as a fellow citizen.

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Vasiljevic liked company or rather that he liked to drink, that he got drunk?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I do know that he was gay, he liked company, and I would frequently see him sitting at a table with friends and he would be known to have a little too much to drink and to get drunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Visegrad is a small town, did you hear from anyone or did you see Mr. Vasiljevic commit any offences, take part in any looting, or demonstrate any other kind of criminal behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything like that, never anything bad about him. I knew him as I said, as a good fellow citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, at any time or place, did you see Mr. Vasiljevic wearing any kind of uniform? If you did, tell us what kind, and did he carry a weapon or something else or did he not carry anything?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As I said already, I told you what kind of clothing I saw him in. I never saw him in any uniform nor with a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard from anyone or did you personally see him participating or involved with any kind of paramilitary formations or not?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your knowledge of Mr. Vasiljevic, could you tell us your opinion, and I'm asking for your opinion, being the kind of man you described him to be, could he have taken part in any such crimes, criminal activities and the like?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know him, and knowing him from before the war, I doubt that he could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you: I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tanaskovic. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:
