utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Novakovic. My name is Dermot Groome and I represent the Office of the Prosecutor and I'm just going to ask you a few questions this afternoon regarding your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you once again to describe, as best you're able, the armband that you say you saw on Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said I would usually pass in a car. He had an armband that was red in colour. Now, whether it had any symbol, I don't know, I didn't notice it whether it could have been a red cross or not, I don't know. I just know that the armband was red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've just used the word "red cross". Do you remember seeing a red cross on it?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was saying. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony here today is that you did not see a red cross on that armband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember giving a statement to Mr. Tanaskovic back in May of the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was on the 5th of May, 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you being as truthful with Mr. Tanaskovic regarding what you remembered regarding this armband at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I said the truth then, and I'm telling the truth now and to the best of my recollection and what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I'm going to show you your statement, I'm going to refer you to a particular sentence and then I'm going to ask you whether you that changes your testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that Prosecution document 110.1 and 110.2, 110.1 being the B/C/S version of the statement and 110.2 being the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I'd ask you to look at the second paragraph of your statement. It begins with the word "Dom," D-o-m, and in about the middle of that paragraph there's a sentence that describes what you say about the red cross. I'd ask you to read that to yourself and you let me know when you've finished.

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that it had a red cross sign on it. Knowing it was red, I thought it was of the Red Cross. I just remembered the red colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony, sir, that when you see the colour red, you immediately think of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't saying that. I just went by and I thought to myself, he might be from the Red Cross. I have always said it was red in colour, now whether there was a sign on it or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you admit or deny that in your statement to Mr. Tanaskovic, you said, "It seems to me that he had the sign of the Red Cross." Do you admit or deny that you said that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I deny that I knew there was a red cross because here there is this phrase, "It seems to me". I'm not denying anything, I'm just not claiming that it was the Red Cross, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What you are being asked to say is that you concede that what was read to you was what you said to the investigator. "It Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. seems to me that he had the sign of the Red Cross." Now, do you agree that is what you said to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I told the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic, on the trip from the Visegrad health centre up to Uzice, did you pass by Mr. Vasiljevic's house?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We went directly along the road leading to Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've also testified about when you believe it was that you made this trip up to Uzice and I want to ask you: When is the first time, after 1992, that somebody asked you: Do you remember when it was you went to Uzice with Mitar Vasiljevic in the ambulance? When was the first time somebody asked you to recall that information?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The first time this question was put to me on the 5th of May by the attorney Mr. Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was approximately eight years after the event; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you recall it right away or did you receive any assistance in recalling when it was that this happened?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No one assisted me. I didn't fix the date then, I just knew it was a religious holiday, a Sunday, and the Troica, the Trinity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you know that it was a religious holiday. Could it have been another religious holiday around that time, St. Vidovdan day or St. Vitus day?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Vidovdan is later, it is at the end of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us how it is eight years later you are so sure it was the first religious holiday and not the second, and I believe they are two weeks apart?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I know when those holidays are celebrated on the same dates, Vidovdan is always the 28th of June and 14 days before that is the Trinity holiday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a clear memory of what you did earlier in the day on Trinity Sunday?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we were under work obligation. There were no holidays. We had to work every day, and you had to go to work. So I was working as I did on any other day and then I came home to rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your shift that day?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have shifts. My working hours were from 8.00 a.m. until 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you leave the health centre directly after your work hours ended or did you remain there afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I went straight home by car. I was resting in my own apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until the time you left the health centre, did you see Mitar Vasiljevic in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At 4.00 was Mr. Savic at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: MOLOJE NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: He was on duty in the health centre as the driver then. Now, whether he was in the centre or in the field, at that depended on whether he was engaged or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TANASKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for coming along to give evidence and for the evidence you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you stand up, please, and take the solemn declaration in the document which the court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sikiric. Would you please get closer to the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you properly and please wait a couple of seconds after my question before giving your answer. Could you please introduce yourself? What is your name, where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: My name is Dobrivoje Sikiric, I was born in the village of Jablanica, Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of June, 1938.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, Mr. Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to wait a couple of seconds before giving your answer because of the interpreters since we are speaking the same language. Will you please tell me your wife's name and her date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: My wife's name is Mileva, she was born on the 20th of February, 1939.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is your wife from, what is her maiden name?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Her maiden name is Marinkovic and she comes from the same village that I was born in, that is, Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live, Mr. Sikiric?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I am now living in Vardiste, Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you been living in Vardiste?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Since 1971.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without any interruption, and were you living in Vardiste in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mitar Vasiljevic personally?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I know Mitar from the day he was born as he was my sister's son. My sister gave birth to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe your relationship in detail?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: My sister is his mother, so I am his uncle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your sister is Mr. Vasiljevic's mother?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is she alive?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No, she's not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did she die?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, Mr. Sikiric, you are married to Milena, do you have children?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I had a son who was killed in this terrible war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you only had one son, you had no other children?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know, Mr. Sikiric, that even now it is hard for you to talk about it, but try and control your emotions and I shall try not to delve into the matter at any length, but I have to ask you a few questions about the time when your son was killed and do forgive me for having to do that though I know it must be very hard on you. What was your occupation at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I was a caterer with my own business, that was always my occupation and it is still to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is this establishment that you own?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: It is in Vardiste, Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where, in the village, is that restaurant situated?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: It is close to the border with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the main road, the Visegrad-Uzice road?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: It is on that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you, the establishment is right on the road?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Sikiric, that you had an only son and that he was killed in the war. Could you tell us when he was killed and what was his name?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: His name was Zeljko Sikiric, he was killed on the 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was killed and under which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: He was killed on the road between Visegrad to Gorazde, not exactly on the road, above the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your son a soldier or, rather, had he been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had been mobilised to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything further about this, what unit he was in and how far the place where he was killed is from Visegrad or Vardiste?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, it's about ten kilometres away from Visegrad, and there are 20 from Vardiste to Visegrad so all together it would be about 30 kilometres away from our house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was not in the area of Vardiste, but on the opposite side of Visegrad when you add up the kilometres and say it was 30 kilometres from Vardiste, do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same occasion, was it just your son Zeljko who was killed or was somebody else killed at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to ascertain, five of them were killed and my Zeljko was among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the others who were killed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember because I was looking for my child so I took note of everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us what you remember, please?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Radoje Masal from Vardiste, Milko Masal from Vardiste, Dragomir Simsic from Vardiste, Zeljko Sikiric from Vardiste and Djordje Trivkovic who was from the area of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sikiric, did you learn of your son's death on the day he was killed or later?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No, we hoped he would come as he always did in the evening or in the morning but on Tuesday, I became suspicious because there was no word and we had heard that there had been some casualties in the vicinity of Visegrad so I immediately began to suspect, I started asking questions. My car had broken down, but there was a woman from the Masala family who had a car and we took her car and when we arrived there, they found two of them the day after but the other three it took three days to find them and this happened on Monday at about 4.00 p.m., that was when it happened, and we found my son and the two Masal or rather Dragomir Simsic, Mirko Masal and my Zeljko, we found them only on the Thursday of the same week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke of the day, I think you mentioned the day of the week. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: It was Monday, the 1st of June, 1992 that my son was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, your son and two others were not found until Thursday, and their bodies were not pulled out until then?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Sikiric, when the funeral took place, your son's funeral?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: It was on Saturday, the 6th of June, the same year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it an orthodox funeral with the presence of a priest?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he buried?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: He was buried in Vardiste in the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mitar Vasiljevic present at the funeral?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He came with his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his wife's name?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Milojka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you something in connection with Serbian customs. Is it customary when someone dies or is killed for relatives and friends to come to the house to express their condolences?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, that week, they all came when I was looking for my son, they all came to the house to ask what was new. And when my son was found on Thursday, our family came, everybody wanted to know what had happened. They came from Belgrade. My wife's brothers came from -- because my son had six uncles, they came, Mitar Vasiljevic also came. I think it was on Friday, and that was when the preparations were being made for the funeral, according to our customs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your answer to my question was yes, it was the custom and many people did come and you mentioned the various family members and others who came, among them you mentioned Mitar Vasiljevic. Does that mean that he came to your house to express his condolences before the funeral?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Sikiric, that he came to the funeral with his wife Milojka?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were probably many people there and you were probably feeling very bad, but I still ask you whether you remember what his reaction was and how he behaved?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, I can answer that. As you can imagine, this was a tragic event for me, but I saw that Mitar was very sad at my son's funeral. He was thoughtful as were all our relatives and all the family, and that's usual in the cases of tragedy like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not go any further into this. I realise that it must be very hard for you to talk about it. I will now ask you the following: You said that you ran a cafe at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have your own car?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you travel at that time in order to bring supplies for your cafe, because I assume that you couldn't get them in Vardiste?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, because I'm 20 kilometres away from Visegrad, and that unfortunate war was going on at the time, there was nothing to be bought. I was the only one whose establishment was open, and there was nothing to be had in Visegrad, so I went to Serbia constantly to buy supplies for my establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Visegrad is about 20 kilometres away from your house. How far is Uzice from Vardiste?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: A little over 50 kilometres from my house, about 55 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you still went to Uzice to get supplies even though it was further away than Visegrad because, as you said, there were shortages of goods in Visegrad. What did you mean by saying that it was not a safe road?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not safe. There was no security. It was not safe, you couldn't pass and also, there were no goods to be bought in Visegrad so sometimes I went to Uzice as many as two times a day and I would get goods, sometimes more, sometimes less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, at that time, I am speaking of the time just before and just after your son's death, you had no reason to go to Visegrad, did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not go to Visegrad at all after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now go back to your encounter with Mitar Vasiljevic on the 6th of June which was a Saturday, he came to your son's funeral with his wife?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember when was the next time you saw him and how soon after that it was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: We didn't see each other after that for a brief time. My son was buried on the 6th of July and then I stopped going to Visegrad. We went to the cemetery every day as was the customary and I saw Zivorad Savic and Miloje. I was surprised, and they said to me, "Here is Mitar. Here is your nephew. He's broken his leg. There he is in the ambulance." And I was amazed. I came out and I saw him and they said to me, "Mitar says he's cold," so I called my wife, my late wife. She died a year after my son was killed, and she brought a blanket. We took it outside and gave it to Mitar to cover himself, and the others came in and had a drink. They stayed a brief while, and then they took Mitar to Uzice and I stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sikiric, can you remember in relation to the date you remember well, Saturday, the 6th of June, the day of the funeral, how much time passed until the day when you saw Mitar Vasiljevic again in the circumstances you have just described?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many days it was. I worked every day even on Sundays, but it may have been seven or eight days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was your first encounter with him after the day of the funeral?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what time of day it was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was in the afternoon, just before nightfall. There was still quite a lot of daylight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to the occasion when they came to your house?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say how long they stayed in your cafe?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, they had coffee, they waited for us to make coffee, we had a chat. I can't tell you how long it was. I never look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they or Mitar, did any one of them tell you how it came about that Mitar had this accident?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, they said he had fallen off a horse. I suppose he had a horse somewhere. I was surprised to hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they said," who do you mean when you say "they"?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Savic and Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you talked to them first?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, they came in. I didn't know anything about it. They came in and they said, "There's your nephew. He's fallen off a horse and broken his leg. We're taking him to Uzice."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went outside and saw Mitar in the vehicle, what did you discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I asked him, "Mitar, how did this happen?" And he told me. I found it odd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Sikiric, "that you found it odd," what do you mean? What was odd?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, it was odd for him to fall off a horse -- how shall I put it -- maybe he didn't know how to ride. I don't know what happened. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you are -- you were related through your sister, I don't know how often you saw each other, but did you know anything about whether he liked horses or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything special about it, but I know his grandfather and his father had horses when Mitar was a young boy. I knew that, and I knew that he could ride when I went to visit them. That's why I was so surprised that he should fall off a horse, that he should not be able to command a horse properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conversation with him on that occasion, did you can ask him about the reaction of his family to this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't discuss that with him. I don't remember having discussed it with him at any rate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss it with anyone from his family after he left?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as they left for Uzice, I called Milojka and I wanted to know whether she knew about this or not, so I called her. I said, "Milojka, do you know what happened?" to warn her, because when someone is missing, when someone doesn't come home, people are afraid. So I said to my wife, "Let's call Milojka right away so that she won't worry, so that she'll just know that he's just broken his leg, that it's not something worse."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your conversation with her, were you able to gather that it was from you she learned of this or that she already knew about it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Milojka didn't know. She was surprised, and then she said, "Is that all?" And I said, "It's all. He's just broken his leg. Zika and the other man told me that he had just broken his leg, so trust us." She was afraid that something worse had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that her reaction was, "Is that all that's happened?" Do you mean that she was afraid that the injury was worse and that you were keeping it from her?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the vehicle went on in the direction of Uzice, can you say whether the time of day had changed?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: How do you mean "changed"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The time that they spent at your place and when they left, was it still daylight or twilight?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: There was still daylight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit Mitar Vasiljevic while he was in hospital in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did quite often, perhaps not every time I went to Uzice because I went there often to get supplies, but I did visit him once a week, perhaps, or maybe even twice a week sometimes, but at least once a week I went to see how he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what ward he was in when you visited him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, the first time I visited him, he was in the orthopaedic ward, and he had weights on his leg, traction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could he get up or move around?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No, how could he get up when he had weights attached to his leg?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he was in the orthopaedic ward, did he later move to another ward?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, he was transferred. I went to see him and they said he's not here anymore. They knew me, a lot of doctors and nurses in the Uzice hospital knew me because my wife had been a patient there, that's why they knew me so I asked where he was and they said, "He's gone to the psychiatric ward." And I found him there because I knew a lot of nurses so they let me through and they allowed me to see him. It wasn't really possible for everyone, but I managed, and when I came to see him in the psychiatric ward, I noticed that he was out of his mind in a manner of speaking, and I was very disturbed by this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what this looked like, why you had this impression when you say he was out of his mind. Can you describe in greater detail what was happening in your view?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say what the consequences were of the various tragedies that happened. I can't prove anything. I'm not an expert on this. But probably it was because of all the horrors that were happening in Visegrad and maybe he was very upset because his cousin had been killed in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for your reply, but that wasn't what I was asking you. I didn't ask you for your opinion about the causes of this, but I asked you what you noticed, what made you think that something was wrong?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Now I understand. I came to see him and I would always bring him something, and I started talking to him but his answers had nothing to do with my questions. That's what I noticed that he was saying things that had nothing to do with the conversation between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to ask him questions and to get replies to them?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't able to do that because I saw that he didn't understand what I was asking him. He didn't understand what I was saying so I couldn't correct him. It was a very tricky situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 24 25 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sikiric, let us resume with your testimony. The last point we were discussing were your visits to Mitar Vasiljevic at the hospital. Mr. Sikiric, do you know who took Mitar Vasiljevic out of hospital when his treatment was over?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: When the treatment was over, Milojka, his wife, called me that we go and fetch him from hospital. So I went to Uzice with Milojka and drove Mitar back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you drove him, you probably mean in your own car.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mitar Vasiljevic have a car?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No, he never had a car, nor did he drive, nor did he ever pass a driving test.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Sikiric, that Mitar Vasiljevic underwent treatment before this, and if you know, tell us of what?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before that period, maybe seven or eight years ago, he was admitted to the same ward with some mental problems. He wasn't healthy mentally, as I would put it. I don't know how to express myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "at the same ward," you mean the ward from which he was discharged in Uzice?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember, it was a long time ago, but he was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which hospital are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: The one in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why this condition set in for which he underwent treatment?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: We all had our suspicions. As he worked for years as a caterer, he liked to have too much to drink, and maybe it's genetic too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever with him when he had had too much to drink?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes I was in his company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would he behave then?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Under the influence of alcohol, he would not be aggressive. He would be cheerful and made jokes, but after that came the problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that after this period that you were referring to, 1992 in Uzice, that is, do you know whether he went to hospital again after that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, a year later, he broke a leg again, I don't know which one it was. So sometime in 1993 or 1994, he spent all summer there. He had spinal surgery. I took him to Belgrade where he underwent surgery. I went to visit him in Belgrade too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the exception of the period he spent in hospital and when he underwent treatment in 1992, 1993, and 1994, do you know what was his profession at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: He was working in catering establishments, but even while working, he would often be drunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, after this period, was he permanently employed or was there a period when there was no work?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to Visegrad that often afterwards, but there wasn't work all the time continuously, but I don't know what else he could have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Being yourself in the catering business, did you work at fairs, religious holidays, under a tent, organising festivities of that kind?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is done regularly. Ever since I started working as a private caterer in 1978, as Mitar is closely related to me, he would always be around and he has a lot of experience as a waiter. He was my right hand for these fairs, and occasionally, he would stand in for one of my own workers when he was off or when my workers were off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of your bar or coffee bar at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: It was called The Merry Bosnian Lady.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one final question for you. You spoke about his character a little, but I would like you to tell us to the best of your knowledge whether he was a man prone to violence, revenge, the settling of accounts, of any other criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: As far as I know Mitar, I always called him "my Mitar," as I was his uncle. He was never like that. He did a job that suited him. He wasn't aggressive. He liked company. We are all like that, and that's how Mitar was too. He was well seen in any company. When I worked at these fairs, he would bring his colleagues to help, regardless of their religion, whether they were Serbs or Muslims. He would bring his whole crew to come and work for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And finally, could the witness be shown Defence Exhibit D19.1. D19 is in English, D19.1 in B/C/S. And could D14.1 be prepared also and be shown to the witness immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at the Exhibit D19.1. Is that a death certificate for your son Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you also now look at the second document, D14.1. It's a certificate. And please confirm whether that is correct.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I personally asked the priest to issue me this, because a priest was in Vardiste, and then the religious books were transferred to a monastery 5 kilometres away, the Dobrun monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you recognise that document yourself?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I requested that document, and I personally also received it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sikiric. Cross-examined by Ms. Bauer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sikiric. My name is Sabine Bauer, and I'm appearing on behalf of the Prosecution. I'd like to ask you several questions regarding your testimony. Mr. Sikiric, when was the first time you were asked to recall the events of today that you recalled from that time, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: You mean to tell you about the events in 1992. The attorney Rade asked me, as I know quite a bit about it, and that is why he asked me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time --

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: -- to testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, did you give a statement to Mr. Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us today that you would go and get your supplies from Uzice, and sometimes you would get those supplies nearly twice a day. Now, my question for you is: Would you go alone in your car to Uzice when you were getting your supplies?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I always go alone. If I have a passenger, then I can't carry enough supplies. Or if I'm transporting a relative or somebody who needs help, who needs a lift to Uzice, I take them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992, you told us the road was rather dangerous at that time to travel, but you didn't feel you had to take anybody along for your protection, did you?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: The road was dangerous from Vardiste to Visegrad, to the west. And my house is 200 metres from the border, from the Yugoslav border nowadays the Serbian border, present-day Yugoslavia. So I didn't know anybody to go with me when I would cross the border after 200 metres and enter Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take you by car to drive to Uzice?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: The road is quite good, and if the road is dry, I can make it in 40 to 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us today that your bar was open seven days a week in 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked every day, as I was quite some distance from Visegrad, on the very Yugoslav border, so that they allowed me to work because I wasn't close to the critical points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you also worked on holidays and Christian holidays during that time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, because it's a catering establishment that works every day, that is open every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told us that after your son died, you visited the cemetery on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, almost every day, especially the first seven days. That is the custom. And the cemetery is 50 metres from my house. And I had my own workers. I was running the business and the workers were working in the shop, mostly women in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you continue to visit the cemetery after that regularly as well?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to our customs, at first you go every week at the beginning, and nowadays ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, am I correct in saying that after so much time, you can't be absolutely sure anymore how many days after the funeral Mitar Vasiljevic came to your house; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: That is correct. That's what I said. I can't remember the exact day, but it was around about those days, that is, shortly after my tragedy, my son's death and his funeral. So it was around about then, about mid-June. I said about seven or eight days later, but those who drove him, they will remember better, those who testified before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us when he came by, he remained in the ambulance and you were told about his fall from a horse, and then you saw him and he told you about it, how it came about. What, precisely, did he tell you what did happen to him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: He told me, "Uncle, I fell off a horse."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you inquire with him how it happened or how come that it happened since you knew he was an experienced horseback rider in his youth?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember. I almost laughed and I said, "How come you fell when you know how to ride?" Nothing more than that. I didn't ask him how he fell, at least I don't remember asking him about the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he didn't tell you anything about who he got the horse from and how he came about to ride the horse, et cetera; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did he ask you for anything to drink?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I seem to remember that we took him out something, my wife and I, to have something to drink. Now, what it was, I don't know, but we did. And the others who walked through the door said, "Take something for Mitar to drink."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in total, he appeared to you quite normal, sober, not drunk that day?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I couldn't notice whether he had been drinking or not, but it was an accident and he wasn't in a good mood, of course. You know how it is when you have a broken leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you for alcohol?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Even if he had asked me for it, I wouldn't have given it to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you also visited Mr. Vasiljevic while he was in the orthopaedic ward in the Uzice hospital. Did you have conversations Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with him at that time when you were bringing him some little things?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk to him, and to the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he, at that time, tell you maybe what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I knew that he had fallen off a horse. I knew that. We probably talked about it. He fell, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, the conversations you had with him were not out of the ordinary, would you say; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No. We spoke about family things and about this, his problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you told us then also today that he sort of was out of his mind when he was brought to the psychiatric ward, and you said specifically you estimate not that you can prove it because it was of all the horrors that happened in Visegrad at that time. Did he tell you anything about all the horrors that he might have witnessed in Visegrad at that time? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: What I mean is because he wasn't answering my questions. I would say one thing and he would answer something quite disconnected, and that is why I came to the conclusion that he wasn't answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you concluded it was based either because he was also so upset about your cousin's [sic] death or because of all the horrors that happened in Visegrad at that time. What made you say "all the horrors that happened in Visegrad at that time"?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the horrors, the killing of the five men in a single day, in a single hour. Because while the Yugoslav army was there, Muslims and Serbs were together and nobody was killed. The first to be killed were these five men in Visegrad. None of the Muslims got killed before them. Yes, one did, a month, I think, later, Selim, but these were the first to get killed in Visegrad, and for everybody, everybody was flabbergasted about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the five men that you are talking about are the five men that were killed together with your son; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can I conclude that up to the psychiatric ward, you didn't notice any difference in Mitar Vasiljevic's behaviour. That was the first time you noticed that he was so-called out of his mind?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: One could see on Mitar that he was drinking more than usual, so it could have been the effect of the alcohol too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- but what I meant was it was the first time that you saw a difference in his behaviour when you saw him at the psychiatric ward. That's the only thing I wanted to clear up.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, at the funeral of my son, whether he was really drunk, he probably was drunk. He was disturbed. I could notice this, but I couldn't pay more attention because there were a lot of people present. It was a surprise for everyone that so many should be killed in one day. And when I arrived at the psychiatric ward, I realised and noticed that he had absolutely taken leave of his senses, that he didn't understand what I was saying. He kept talking disconnectedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, talking about the funeral of your son, you say actually his reaction was sad and thoughtful. You didn't say he was drunk. Was he in any way -- did he cry at the funeral?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I was able to see, it wasn't just Mitar that was crying. A lot of people were crying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he expressed his condolences, did he somehow express anger at this death?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would say that your son's death -- Mitar Vasiljevic was very close with your son - to clear this up front - right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So his death upset him pretty much like it upsets any close relative; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your son died in battle against the Muslims, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, there was still no battles. They were in the Territorial Defence, and there was no shooting up until then. No one got killed before these five men. They were killed by the Muslims. And you know that things got worse after that. Not a single Muslim was killed, at least as far as I know, in Visegrad until that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, then, it is correct that your son died at the hands of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: One hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mitar Vasiljevic never said he would like to take revenge after your son's death, did he?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: He never said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sikiric, in answer to this last question by Ms. Bauer, you said that Mitar had never said anything of that kind to you, but you -- your knowledge of Mitar, in addition to the fact that you said that the death of your son upset him a great deal, do you think that he could kill somebody because of that, especially somebody who had nothing to do with the death of your son?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, knowing Mitar Vasiljevic, I don't think he would be capable of doing anything like that. And I know him from way back, and he never took part. None of our ancestors did or any of that kind. Nobody ever took part in any crimes of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question by Ms. Bauer, you also said that at that time, it wasn't a real war and that the five people who were killed, including your son, were the first victims to fall.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first victims. There was a victim on the Muslim side a month prior to that in the centre of town. Well, not actually the centre but the suburbs of town. Whereas the five who were killed were the first victims in Visegrad. None of the Muslims had died up until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you knew.

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that first victim, the Serb that you spoke about, do you remember his surname?

utterances.speaker: DOBRIVOJE SIKIRIC
utterances.text: Well, some people know, but as I'm not from Visegrad, I don't know his name, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sikiric. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, sir. I think that if you haven't been asked any questions, it would be better for you not to say something that is not required. But we are grateful to you for having come along to give evidence and for the evidence which you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Whilst we're waiting for the next witness, I was informed just before we resumed this afternoon that there is a requirement of the Judges to attend a matter at midday tomorrow, so we obviously can't start at 11.30. What I propose is that we start at 1.00 and go through to 2.30, we have a half an hour's break, and we go then from 3.00 until 4.30. But unfortunately, we won't be able to start, I think, safely -- I can't say that we will start before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are waiting, may I inquire from Mr. Domazet. This next witness is the last scheduled witness for this week. May I be advised of the witnesses to be called tomorrow so that I may prepare for this evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, a group of witnesses arrived today. I haven't seen them yet, but I do envisage that among that group of witnesses -- or, rather, if the testimony of Mr. Radomir Vasiljevic is completed tomorrow, then the next witness will be Mrs. Milena Tomasevic. She is a nurse at the neuropsychiatric ward at the general hospital in Uzice. And tomorrow, after talking to the witnesses, I shall come up with a schedule for the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If anything happens, that that particular witness doesn't arrive tomorrow, will you contact Mr. Groome and let him know who you would call as an alternative?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have been told by the service that they have arrived, and that the lady has arrived. They're in The Hague, but I haven't had any contact with them yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you take the solemn declaration in the document which the court usher is now showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sit down, please. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall be asking you questions on behalf of the Defence counsel and -- but as we speak the same language, to facilitate of the work of the interpreters, would you make pauses between my question and your answer. Perhaps you could use the monitor to help you. You will see when the translation is over. Mr. Vasiljevic, would you tell me your full name, date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Radomir Vasiljevic. I was born on the 27th of February, 1952 in the village of Djurevici near Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me where you went to school and what schools you have -- what schooling you have had?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Primary school and secondary school I finished in Visegrad, and the Faculty of Medicine in Belgrade. I did my specialist training in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you reside?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I reside in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you been living there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I have lived in Visegrad practically since I was born with short interruption, of course, when I did my schooling. And when I went -- began studying, I was in Kladanj, but otherwise I've been living in Visegrad since 1987.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since 1987, what jobs have you held?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked as a doctor in the health centre Visegrad, and then since October 1993, I was director of the Visegrad health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave us your particulars and your place of birth, you said the village of Djurevici as your birthplace. Now my next question is: Do you know Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I have known Mitar Vasiljevic since he was born. He's a little younger than me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, as you have the same surname, my next question is the following: Are you related in any way to Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am related to Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you closely related or are you a distant relative? Can you describe how you are related to him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that it is -- I am closely related despite the same surname but, let me put it this way, our great-grandfathers were cousins. They weren't even brothers, but they were cousins of some kind, first or second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So if your great-grandfathers were distant cousins, it would be correct to say that you are very distantly related; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I agree with you there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you say that you have known Mitar Vasiljevic since his young days, could you tell us how you know him, where you saw him, and generally what you know about him and his family?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that I have known Mitar since he was born, practically, and throughout that time, I don't know whether I could make any criticisms of Mitar at all. I know him as a fine man, a very nice and honest man, a peace-loving man. He liked to make merry. He was a jolly person but not -- never in any excessive kind of way. I also know Mitar's whole family. I know his father, his mother, his brothers and sisters, and I can tell you that it is a very, very fine Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and honest family. I also know Mitar's wife and his children and, as they lived in my neighbourhood for a time, I can tell you that they're a fine family and that there is nothing that can be characterised as bad in any way. So nothing that I would find fault with or that would be unacceptable in terms of into human relations or neighbourly relations or relations among family members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him on the basis of his professional work, on the basis of the job he did? Did you know him that way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I know he was a waiter. I know he worked in different catering establishments in Visegrad. And as all the catering establishments belonged to one company, he was an employee of that company, and the company would move their workers from one restaurant to another. So I saw him working in all the different catering establishments and I have nothing particular to say with respect to his work and his conduct at work and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we have touched upon his work, do you know either professionally or otherwise whether he liked to drink?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could say that Vasiljevic was prone to drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever in a situation in which you saw him when he was drunk, when he drank more than he should have, when he got drunk, in fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him in situations of that kind. I have seen Mitar drunk, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how he behaved when he was drunk? What was he like then?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that his behaviour, Mitar Vasiljevic's behaviour was always acceptable. He was always a docile, peace-loving person. He was never prone to be querulous or indulge in excessive behaviour of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about your job now, the work you did then and the work you do now, your work as a doctor, in fact. You have told us that you worked in the health centre throughout, and since 1993, you have held the post of director of the health centre. In view of that, let us go back to the year 1992 and do you recall the month of May of that particular year and what happened in May, or the second half of May, to be more specific? What started happening in Visegrad at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do remember that period of time. I was there. But let me stress that since that time to the present day, a lot of time has gone by, so I have probably forgotten many things by now. So I don't know what you want me to single out in particular with respect to May 1992. The year went by like all the other war years. There was great fear. There was great chaos. There was great deprivation. There were shortages, no fuel, no medicines, no equipment, no cadres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the job that you did, Mr. Vasiljevic, at that time in the health centre, did you admit both Muslim and Serb patients? Were there any problems in your work regarding the admission of these patients?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The health centre, before 1992, during 1992, and after 1992 admitted absolutely everybody who had the need for treatment in the health centre and so there were never any problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period, were you ever in a situation in which you had to offer medical assistance to Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: In May? In May 1992, I don't know whether I did in the health centre, whether I helped him in the health centre, but I did extend assistance to Mitar Vasiljevic. It might have been in May, the end of May or the beginning of June, but not in the health centre itself. This was in Uzamnica, in the barracks, where the Yugoslav People's Army was put up before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't specifically thinking about the health centre. I meant in general. So you say you did have occasion to give him medical assistance in Uzamnica at the end of May, beginning of June. Do you happen to remember how this came about and what happened? How did you help him with your medical intervention?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was - and let me stress that a lot of time has gone by since then - from a call by Captain Kovacevic. He made two calls in the course of the day. He phoned the outpatient department of the health clinic. I was working there. And in the evening perhaps -- it might have been 9.00 or 8.00. 8.00 or 9.00, thereabouts. I know it was night-time. It was dark. You couldn't see anything. I went to the Uzamnica barracks. And Captain Kovacevic over the phone had told me that it was a relative of mine, Mitar Vasiljevic, he was calling about, that he was undergoing a psychological crisis and that he -- and that medical assistant was necessary. He refused to eat. He was refusing his food. He was behaving in a strange way, at least as far as Kovacevic was able to assess, and that's why he called me and that's why I went, taking a nurse with me. We went to the Uzamnica barracks, and as I say, before the war it was used as a barracks. When I got there, I found Mitar Vasiljevic in the building that they called the command, the headquarters. So I came in first, and then they brought Mitar Vasiljevic in several minutes later, and I examined him, and we did what was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you didn't go into the room in which he was in, but they brought him to a building which was the headquarters of the command, which is where you were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. When I went in through the gate, I went some 50 metres to a building which they called the command, and several minutes later, they brought in Mitar Vasiljevic. So I didn't visit -- I didn't go to the room in which Mitar had been in up until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the Uzamnica barracks as being a barracks used by the JNA before the war, but you didn't tell us what it was used as at the time you were there.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war, the premises was used by the JNA as a weapons depot. And in the period that I was there, as I was later told and as I was to learn later on, it was a camp of some kind, a prison in which prisoners of war were held, and also our soldiers were there who were serving a sentence of some kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said that later on. But at the time you were there, when you went at the end of May or beginning of June, did you know what it was used for? Did you know what the former Uzamnica barracks were serving as? Did you know that then?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I knew that Mitar Vasiljevic was there. I didn't know anything else, what it was all about, or what purposes the barracks were used for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know in what capacity Mitar Vasiljevic was there? Why was he there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I learnt that when talking to this man Kovacevic, and also when I talked to the man who brought me and the nurse back to the health centre or from the Uzamnica barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they tell you? What did they say?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: They said that Mitar was there as a prisoner and that he was in prison because he had had some differences of opinion with his superiors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had heard that from the man called Kovacevic and another man who had come with you, who came with you on that occasion, who accompanied you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The nurse and I were accompanied from the health centre to the

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know where he worked at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he worked and what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, before that period of 1992, did the town of Visegrad have its prison, whatever type of prison for misdemeanours or offences of any kind? Did it have a prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Visegrad at one time did have some kind of prison for minor offenders and sentencing and probably an investigations prison, but whether it functioned or not and how long it functioned, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long Mitar Vasiljevic had been in Uzamnica before you came, before the day that you came to visit as a physician?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: From talking to Kovacevic, I learnt that he had been there for two days or several days. I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were there, did anybody happen to say how long he would be staying in prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: After I examined him, after I examined Vasiljevic and after I talked to him, which was the decisive part, I came to the conclusion that it would be far better for Vasiljevic if he were to be released because they told me that he hadn't committed any major offence and that is why -- that is what I proposed. I said to Kovacevic that his state, his psychological state would improve if he were to be released. And Kovacevic promised that he'd see what he could do and that he would release him either that very evening or the next day. Now, whether that was actually done, I don't know. I didn't inquire after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that, does that mean that you don't actually know when he was, in fact, released from the Uzamnica prison?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I do know that after my -- after my visit to Uzamnica, he was released. Whether it was that very evening or the next day or the day after, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, did you have occasion a few days later to see Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that I didn't see Mitar Vasiljevic very often because of my work at the health centre and how busy we were, but I did have occasion to see Mitar seven or eight days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that particular occasion and could you describe it when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't any special situation. I saw Mitar in the street with a group of men, of people, cleaning, collecting glass, as far as I recollect. You could hear the sound of broken glass. And a group of people were tearing down posters and trying to wash away the graffiti on some of the buildings in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mitar Vasiljevic doing? What were you able to notice him doing when you saw him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I had the impression that he was organising these people to work. He had some kind of leadership role in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you had the impression, on what basis did you gain such an impression?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Probably because just then, he was wearing some kind of an armband on his sleeve which is usually worn by people on duty at various events. So I -- it was probably on that basis that I concluded that he was some sort of an organiser of the group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what kind of an armband that was?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was a red armband, the colour was red.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he wearing this armband?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: On his upper arm. I don't know whether it was his left or his right arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice on that armband anything else? Was there any symbol or any other colour apart from the one you told us about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember seeing anything else. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether Mitar Vasiljevic was armed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He wasn't armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember what kind of clothing he was wearing, of course if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you with any precision what kind of clothing it was, but to the best of my recollection, it was dark clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing and recognising anyone else in that group of people working with him on the cleaning?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember having recognised anyone else in the group. I passed by very quickly. I didn't stay. I didn't linger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only occasion that you saw him doing that kind of work or did you see him on some other occasion as well, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him on any other occasion, though I had heard from others that Mitar Vasiljevic was organising the cleaning of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember who it was from. Probably people who came to the health centre and who passed through the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the comments those people were making about these cleaning activities? Did they speak about it favourably or unfavorably. Did they talk of any problems or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: These were mostly positive reactions, favourable ones, because, you see, in that period of time, no one would have cleaned the rubbish from town if he hadn't taken on the task. Now, whether he did so on his own initiative or whether he received orders from someone to do that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you rarely passed the town's centre because you were very busy. Was it your duty -- was your duty as a doctor also a work obligation or a military assignment, and what kind of obligations did you have in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'll have to elaborate a little to explain. You see, since the war broke out, on the basis of the law and organisationally, there was a vacuum. There were no instructions, no doctrine, no orders, no information, so that we had to find our way around, and we did what we thought was best at that point in time. In fact, you could say that the staff of the health centre self-organised themselves, and we did so in such a way that we spent most of our time at the health centre itself. We were short of doctors, short of staff, short of nurses. We would go home more or less one day a week, and we would spend the rest of the time at the health centre working whenever it was necessary, without any fixed working hours. I have to tell you that the health centre, throughout the time of the war, was a civilian institution. Never for a moment was it a military institution. But we did also treat members of the army, officers, soldiers, the wounded, and the injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A doctor's intervention, examinations and everything else, were they remunerated; that is, did patients have to pay for these services?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely all the services given by the health centre were free of charge. It was out of the question to ask for payment for services rendered by the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is as far as the patients were concerned. Was it normal to send invoices, to send those bills to a medical -- either a medical institution or a military administration? How did this work at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: You see, according to the system of health insurance that was in place in socialist Yugoslavia, all citizens were covered, and they were fully covered. Everyone was entitled to treatment free of charge. And we would just take down the particulars of citizens, and then the services rendered to the citizens who applied to the health centre were then -- the bills were sent to the health insurance fund and then we would obtain remuneration from them. With the war, all this fell apart. And I must tell you that it was only in 1993 that we learnt that there was a health ministry that was functioning in Republika Srpska. So that the whole organisation collapsed, and our health centre, as an institution is mainly financed, if I can put it like that, by the municipality and through humanitarian aid. But in any event, all the services are free of charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, how did you keep records of patients who came to be examined at your health centre?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That, too, is something that is prescribed by law, how you keep records. However, in wartime, we continued the same method we had applied before the war by inertia. So that the method of keeping records remain the same, starting from the protocol, the referral documents, and so on.
