So the aim is to have written evidence of when somebody came, why he came, what the diagnosis was, what was administered to the patient as therapy, whether it's an injection, when he received it, how much medication he received, and so on. So one could say that the protocols are the basic documents of health institutions, and they continue to be that today, fundamental documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the protocol is the fundamental document, that it was that then and still is today, does that mean that all patients have to be registered in that protocol, that protocol of patients?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what that means. Whoever comes for an examination, whoever is given any kind of service in the health centre, their names are registered in the protocol or book of records, and this is kept as a permanent document. And there are legal provisions regulating the safekeeping of these records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this apply to the health centre in Visegrad of which you are now the director? Do you keep protocols from the past, from earlier years?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All protocols in the health centre, and those that have been filled in since I have been director, are kept in the health centre and are readily available. I can tell you that people who lose their medical documents are able to claim certain benefits on the basis of certain health problems, whether they were wounded, or injured, or had some serious illnesses, they address the health centre and we issue them official certificates on the basis of that protocol, and then they can use those documents to further claim benefits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one of the reasons, in addition to the legal obligation to keep such records, is also to help in proving certain facts, certain treatment that patients underwent in a certain period of time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the protocol which you said was the fundamental or basic document, were there any other records? Were there patient forms or cards or not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: These cards did exist, but those cards existed or index cards for people who were treated at the health centre for housewives, for children, for the employed. But during the war, there were people who applied to the health centre for the first time, and we didn't have any cards for them. They had not been registered. When you take down all the particulars that you need to take down in these cards, then you still have to do it in the protocol because these cards are handed over to the patient. He can take it from one dispensary to another, from one doctor to another, and it often gets lost. So one has to have a place where this information is safely kept, and that is why this protocol or book of records exists in our medical system ever since I have been a part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, as opposed to these cards on which particulars are also written, but these cards move around and are often given to patients to take from one doctor to another, everything has to be written down in the protocol and it is stationary, it always stays in the institution, it isn't taken anywhere?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. But in the card, you usually have far more information than in the protocol because there's very little space available per patient in the protocol. So that the protocol would usually contain the diagnosis, the therapy, and whether he was sent on for further treatment somewhere else, whether he would be transported by ambulance or by public transport, also whether the therapy was administered, the therapy prescribed, or whether he was given pills or tablets, and then you will find in the protocol that the patient was given prescriptions and that he would get the medicines in the pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who writes down the information in the protocol?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I never saw a rule about that which would prescribe whose duty it was, but I can tell you how it's done in practice. The particulars are usually written down by the examining doctor or, rather, a part of it, the part relating to the diagnosis, whereas the name, surname, and particulars of the patient are written down by the nurse. And when the patient is given the prescriptions by the doctor, then the nurse fills in, copies from the prescription what has been prescribed to the patient in the protocol. So there are some entries that are filled in by doctors and some by nurses. It often happens for the doctor to ask the nurse for her to fill it in, the doctor will just dictate the diagnosis and everything else and then the nurse will just write it down. So there's no rigid rule about that, hard and fast rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The registration of patients in the protocol, is it done by chronological order, that is, one day after another when the patient appears for examination?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, chronologically, and if you open a protocol, you will see that the numbers are strictly in order. It is not allowed to make any entries in between two patients. If a mistake is made, according to rules on corrections, I'm not sure which law it was, but if you had to make a correction, you would have to cross out the previous information in such a way that it continues to be visible and legible and then the correction has to be certified by a stamp and signature of the person making the correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the procedure if a correction needs to be made in the protocol, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the protocol had an ordinal number. And did it also have to indicate the date when the patient appeared?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so. A date was essential.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then came the information you told us about, the personal particulars of the patient, diagnosis, medicines, and where he was referred to. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was there another -- any other book of records in which a record was kept of emergency calls and when ambulances would go to deal with these calls? I'm talking about the 1992 period.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There was never any such book of records in the health centre before the war, during the war, and also not in the period you're Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. referring to. If I remember well, no such provision ever existed regulating the need for such a book of records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, it might be a convenient time to actually tender the book that the Prosecution has been looking at. What number had you intended to give to it? You have some blank numbers there, but they may be saved for something. The next number up is 24, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 26, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Twenty-six.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I should like to tender it as D26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The Visegrad Hospital protocol book will be Exhibit D26. Now, we will resume tomorrow at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 23rd day of November, 2001, at 1.00 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
